# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is a book about making decisions with AI.

Every day, software makes millions of small decisions: whether a message is a scam, which team should handle a complaint, whether a payment is safe, or whether an AI agent should take an action. More and more of these decisions are now given to large language models like ChatGPT. LLMs are excellent at reading and writing, but a decision is not a paragraph of text. It is a choice between a few options, made without being fully sure, and every wrong choice has a cost.

To make such decisions well, you need three things:

- a **probability you can trust**, which means what it says;
- a **threshold based on the cost of mistakes**, not on habit;
- a clear rule for **when to hand the case to a person**.

Most people building with AI today do not have all three. This book explains each of them from the beginning, in simple language, without any code.

In 2026, a company called TypeSafe AI released Jev, which it calls the first **System One model**: a model that never writes text, and only answers clear questions with probabilities, in one fast step [@typesafe2026]. This book shows how to judge such a model for yourself. But the main idea is bigger than any one product: decisions deserve their own fast, testable layer in an AI system, and that layer needs its own skills.

## How to trust the numbers in this book

**The examples are assumed.** The book follows one imagined company, Kestrel Logistics, and its security team. All numbers about this company are from an assumed example, chosen to explain the ideas clearly. Charts made this way are marked **synthetic**.

**Jev's numbers are illustrations.** The numbers shown for Jev are examples to explain how such a model can be tested, not measurements of the real product.

**Company claims are labelled.** When the book reports what TypeSafe says about Jev, such as its speed or price, it is marked *vendor-reported*, and the source is given.

**Every claim goes into one of three groups:** what can be checked, what the company says, and what nobody outside the company knows yet. Chapter 7 explains this habit. It is a good habit for anything you read about new AI models, including this book.
